claim: The SARS-CoV-2 Delta variant began to cause increases in cases, hospitalizations, and deaths in parts of the United States in Spring 2021.
source: In Spring 2021, the highly transmissible SARS-CoV-2 Delta variant began to cause increases in cases, hospitalizations, and deaths in parts of the United States.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the timing and impact of the Delta variant in the US, presented as established fact in the abstract.

claim: An ensemble of nine mechanistic models produced 6-month scenario projections for July–December 2021 for the United States.
source: As part of the COVID-19 Scenario Modeling Hub, an ensemble of nine mechanistic models produced 6-month scenario projections for July–December 2021 for the United States.
evidence: This describes the methodology used in the study, which is documented throughout the manuscript.

claim: The projections estimated substantial resurgences of COVID-19 across the US resulting from the more transmissible Delta variant.
source: These projections estimated substantial resurgences of COVID-19 across the US resulting from the more transmissible Delta variant, projected to occur across most of the US, coinciding with school and business reopening.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the projection results from the modeling ensemble.

claim: Reaching higher vaccine coverage in July–December 2021 reduced the size and duration of the projected resurgence substantially.
source: The scenarios revealed that reaching higher vaccine coverage in July–December 2021 reduced the size and duration of the projected resurgence substantially, with the expected impacts was largely concentrated in a subset of states with lower vaccination coverage.
evidence: This is a finding from the scenario modeling comparing different vaccination coverage levels.

claim: The magnitude of the Delta wave was substantially underestimated by the models compared with the reported cases, hospitalizations, and deaths occurring during July–December 2021.
source: Despite accurate projection of COVID-19 surges occurring and timing, the magnitude was substantially underestimated 2021 by the models compared with the of the reported cases, hospitalizations, and deaths occurring during July–December, highlighting the continued challenges to predict the evolving COVID-19 pandemic.
evidence: This is a comparison between model projections and observed data, representing a key finding of the study.

claim: Higher vaccination goals at the onset of the surge were estimated to avert over 1.5 million cases and 21,000 deaths.
source: Higher vaccination goals at the onset of the surge of the new variant were estimated to avert over 1.5 million cases and 21,000 deaths, although may have had even greater impacts, considering the underestimated resurgence magnitude from the model.
evidence: This is a quantitative estimate from the scenario modeling comparing different vaccination scenarios.

claim: Reported COVID-19 cases in the US reached a nadir in June 2021.
source: The rapid development, scale-up, and deployment of COVID-19 vaccines in the United States (US) has been one of the biggest public health successes in the US during this pandemic, with reported cases in a nadir in June 2021 (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, 2021b), despite increased testing capacities.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to CDC data.

claim: Non-pharmaceutical interventions (NPIs) including mask mandates were lifted in almost every jurisdiction across the US in Spring 2021.
source: With this success, non-pharmaceutical interventions (NPIs) were lifted, including mask mandates, in almost every jurisdiction across the US in Spring 2021.
evidence: This is a factual statement about policy changes in the US during Spring 2021.

claim: The COVID-19 Scenario Modeling Hub was established in December 2020.
source: Established in December 2020, the COVID-19 Scenario Modeling Hub is an effort to apply a multiple-model approach to produce six-month projections of the state and national trajectories of cases, hospitalizations, and deaths in the US under defined scenarios (Borchering et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a factual statement about when the modeling hub was established, supported by a citation.

claim: In the most pessimistic scenario (70% vaccination coverage and 60% higher variant transmissibility), the resurgence was projected to peak at 414,000 weekly cases and 5900 weekly deaths nationally.
source: In the scenario that assumes lower vaccination coverage among eligible individuals (70%) and higher variant transmissibility (the most pessimistic scenario), this resurgence was projected to peak at 414,000 weekly cases (95% projection interval (PI): 140,000–1,525,000) and 5900 weekly deaths (95% PI: 900–30,000) nationally.
evidence: This is a specific quantitative projection result from the modeling ensemble.

claim: The most pessimistic scenario projected 7,554,000 cumulative cases and 96,000 cumulative deaths during July 4, 2021–Jan 1, 2022.
source: Overall, this scenario projected 7,554,000 (95% PI: 3,294,000–28,399,000) cumulative cases and 96,000 (95% PI: 27,000–476,000) cumulative deaths during July 4, 2021–Jan 1, 2022 (Figure 1).
evidence: This is a specific quantitative projection result from the modeling ensemble, with reference to Figure 1.

claim: With an increase in national vaccine coverage to 80% by January 1, 2022, the ensemble projected 65,000 (16%) fewer cases and 1300 (21%) fewer deaths per week at the peak compared to 70% vaccination coverage.
source: With an increase in national vaccine coverage to 80% by January 1, 2022, the ensemble projected 65,000 (16%) fewer cases and 1300 (21%) fewer deaths per week at the peak, and 1,525,000 (20%) and 21,000 (22%) fewer cumulative cases and deaths, respectively, during July 4, 2021–January 1, 2022, when compared to the scenario where vaccination saturated at 70% nationally (Figure 1).
evidence: This is a comparison of projection results between two vaccination scenarios.

claim: The ten states with the largest projected increases in incidence relative to their winter 2020–21 peak were Louisiana, Hawaii, Nevada, Arkansas, Florida, Missouri, Georgia, Alabama, Alaska, and Arizona.
source: The ten states with the largest projected increases in incidence relative to their winter 2020–21 peak were, in descending order, Louisiana, Hawaii, Nevada, Arkansas, Florida, Missouri, Georgia, Alabama, Alaska, and Arizona.
evidence: This is a specific finding from the state-level projection analysis.

claim: The 10 states with the largest projected resurgences had median peak levels of weekly incident cases that were 18–69% of their winter peak.
source: The ensemble estimates projected these states to experience median peak levels of weekly incident cases that were 18–69% (95% PI: 1%–541%) of their (smoothed) winter peak, although this was exceeded in many states.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the projection analysis comparing projected peaks to historical peaks.

claim: The 10 states with the smallest projected resurgence were Massachusetts, Rhode Island, Vermont, Maine, Minnesota, Pennsylvania, North Dakota, Wisconsin, Tennessee, and South Dakota.
source: The 10 states with the lowest projected resurgences were, in ascending order, Massachusetts, Rhode Island, Vermont, Maine, Minnesota, Pennsylvania, North Dakota, Wisconsin, Tennessee, and South Dakota.
evidence: This is a specific finding from the state-level projection analysis.

claim: The 10 states with the smallest projected resurgence had a median first-dose vaccine coverage of 70% among the eligible population on July 3, 2021, compared to 56% in the ten states with the highest projected resurgence.
source: The 10 states with the smallest projected resurgence had a median first-dose vaccine coverage of 70% among the eligible population (ages 12+) on July 3, 2021, compared to 56% in the ten states with the highest projected resurgence.
evidence: This is a comparison of vaccination coverage data between two groups of states.

claim: There is a high negative correlation (Pearson's r=–0.66) between projected cumulative deaths per population and vaccination coverage on July 3, 2021.
source: We find a high negative correlation (Pearson's r=–0.66, Figure 2) between projected cumulative deaths per population and vaccination coverage on July 3, 2021 (NCIRD, 2021).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the analysis, with reference to Figure 2 and a citation.

claim: In all states, at least 76% of people 65+ had received at least one dose of the vaccine by July 3, 2021.
source: In all states, even those with low overall vaccination coverage, at least 76% of people 65+had received at least one dose of the vaccine, which was expected to have a major effect in limiting mortality from Delta (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, 2021b).
evidence: This is a factual statement about vaccination coverage in the elderly population, supported by a CDC citation.

claim: High vaccination coverage among people 65+ was expected to have a major effect in limiting mortality from Delta.
source: In all states, even those with low overall vaccination coverage, at least 76% of people 65+had received at least one dose of the vaccine, which was expected to have a major effect in limiting mortality from Delta (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, 2021b).
evidence: This is an inference based on vaccination coverage data and knowledge about vaccine effectiveness.

claim: In the 10 states with the largest projected resurgence there was a 9% reduction in the observed case fatality ratio (CFR) comparing August–December 2020 and January–July 2021.
source: The impact of vaccination was already being observed early in the Delta wave: in the 10 states with the largest projected resurgence there was a 9% reduction in the observed case fatality ratio (CFR) comparing August–December 2020 and January–July 2021; in the 10 states with the smallest projected resurgence a 21% reduction in CFR was observed.
evidence: This is a comparison of observed CFR data between two time periods.

claim: In the 10 states with the smallest projected resurgence a 21% reduction in CFR was observed comparing August–December 2020 and January–July 2021.
source: The impact of vaccination was already being observed early in the Delta wave: in the 10 states with the largest projected resurgence there was a 9% reduction in the observed case fatality ratio (CFR) comparing August–December 2020 and January–July 2021; in the 10 states with the smallest projected resurgence a 21% reduction in CFR was observed.
evidence: This is a comparison of observed CFR data between two time periods.

claim: During the projection period, CFR reductions of 15% and 14% were projected compared to August-December 2020.
source: During the projection period, we projected CFR reductions of 15% and 14%, as compared to August-December 2020.
evidence: This is a projection result from the modeling ensemble.

claim: Lower transmissibility variant scenarios projected cumulative national cases of only 9% and 13% compared to the winter 2020–21 peak.
source: Lower transmissibility variant scenarios projected significantly reduced resurgence, projecting cumulative national cases of only 9% and 13% compared to the winter 2020–21 peak.
evidence: This is a projection result from the lower transmissibility scenarios.

claim: In the previous projection round (Round 6), which assumed only a 20% transmissibility increase from a novel variant, resurgence was expected to produce only 8% of the cases reported during the winter 2020–21 peak nationally.
source: Similarly, in the previous projection round (Round 6), which similar to the 7th round except it assumed only a 20% transmissibility increase from a novel variant, resurgence was expected to produce only 8% of the cases reported during the winter 2020–21 peak nationally (COVID-19 Scenario Modeling Hub, 2020).
evidence: This is a comparison to results from a previous projection round, supported by a citation.

claim: Weekly case observations exceeded the 95% projection interval in the first 9 weeks of the projection period in all scenarios.
source: Weekly case observations exceeded our 95% projection interval in the first 9 weeks of the projection period in all scenarios, including those assuming 60% increased transmissibility of the Delta variant (Figure 1).
evidence: This is a comparison between observed data and projection intervals, with reference to Figure 1.

claim: The projections tended to underestimate hospitalizations and deaths in the ascending phase of the Delta wave, although to a lesser degree than cases.
source: Our projections also tended to underestimate hospitalizations and deaths in the ascending phase of the Delta wave, although to a lesser degree.
evidence: This is a comparison between projections and observed data for different outcomes.

claim: The total median projected number of cases underestimated the observed cases during July 4–31, 2021 (1,256,000 observed vs 516,000 projected).
source: The total median projected number of cases underestimated the observed cases overall during this 4-week period (1,256,000 observed vs 516,000 projected); however, we find a strong correlation between ranking of observed and projected total cases per 100,000 during the first four weeks of the projection period, at the state level (Spearman's ⍴=0.87, Figure 3).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison between projected and observed cases, with reference to Figure 3.

claim: There is a strong correlation (Spearman's ⍴=0.87) between ranking of observed and projected total cases per 100,000 during the first four weeks of the projection period at the state level.
source: The total median projected number of cases underestimated the observed cases overall during this 4-week period (1,256,000 observed vs 516,000 projected); however, we find a strong correlation between ranking of observed and projected total cases per 100,000 during the first four weeks of the projection period, at the state level (Spearman's ⍴=0.87, Figure 3).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the analysis comparing state-level rankings, with reference to Figure 3.

claim: Seven of the ten states with greatest projected incidence rank in the ten worst observed incidence states.
source: Seven of the ten states with greatest projected incidence rank in the ten worst observed incidence states.
evidence: This is a finding from comparing projected and observed state rankings.

claim: The two high variant transmissibility scenarios projected the timing of the Delta resurgence, projecting deaths to increase simultaneously with reported cases and peak one week after reported cases.
source: The two high variant transmissibility scenarios, which most closely resembled the characteristics of the circulating Delta variant, projected the timing of the Delta resurgence, projecting deaths to increase simultaneously with reported cases and peak one week after reported cases (Figure 1).
evidence: This is a finding about the timing of projected outcomes, with reference to Figure 1.

claim: At the national level, peak cases were under-projected by 70% and 64% in the two high variant transmissibility scenarios (349,183 and 413,733 vs 1.15 M peak reported weekly cases).
source: Among the two high variant transmissibility scenarios, at the national level the peak cases were under-projected by 70% (95% PI: −25–91%) and 64% (95% PI: −49–88%) (349,183 and 413,733 vs 1.15 M peak reported weekly cases), though the 95% projection interval did capture the reported magnitude of the peak (Figure 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison between projected and observed peak cases, with reference to Figure 1.

claim: The 95% projection interval captured the reported magnitude of the peak cases.
source: Among the two high variant transmissibility scenarios, at the national level the peak cases were under-projected by 70% (95% PI: −25–91%) and 64% (95% PI: −49–88%) (349,183 and 413,733 vs 1.15 M peak reported weekly cases), though the 95% projection interval did capture the reported magnitude of the peak (Figure 1).
evidence: This is a finding about the coverage of projection intervals, with reference to Figure 1.

claim: Hospitalizations were under-projected by 47% and 36% in the two high variant transmissibility scenarios (46,000 and 56,000 vs 87,000 peak reported hospitalizations).
source: Similarly, hospitalizations and deaths were also under-projected by 47% (95% PI: −184–84%) and 36% (95% PI: −230–82%) (46,000 and 56,000 vs 87,000 peak reported hospitalizations) and 67% (95% PI: −77–93%) and 59% (95% PI: −120–93%) (4700 and 6000 vs 14,000 peak reported deaths), respectively; both also captured the reported magnitude within projection intervals.
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison between projected and observed peak hospitalizations.

claim: Deaths were under-projected by 67% and 59% in the two high variant transmissibility scenarios (4700 and 6000 vs 14,000 peak reported deaths).
source: Similarly, hospitalizations and deaths were also under-projected by 47% (95% PI: −184–84%) and 36% (95% PI: −230–82%) (46,000 and 56,000 vs 87,000 peak reported hospitalizations) and 67% (95% PI: −77–93%) and 59% (95% PI: −120–93%) (4700 and 6000 vs 14,000 peak reported deaths), respectively; both also captured the reported magnitude within projection intervals.
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison between projected and observed peak deaths.

claim: The projection intervals for hospitalizations and deaths captured the reported magnitude within projection intervals.
source: Similarly, hospitalizations and deaths were also under-projected by 47% (95% PI: −184–84%) and 36% (95% PI: −230–82%) (46,000 and 56,000 vs 87,000 peak reported hospitalizations) and 67% (95% PI: −77–93%) and 59% (95% PI: −120–93%) (4700 and 6000 vs 14,000 peak reported deaths), respectively; both also captured the reported magnitude within projection intervals.
evidence: This is a finding about the coverage of projection intervals for hospitalizations and deaths.

claim: Prevalence of the SARS-CoV-2 Delta variant rose quickly in the US between May and June 2021, with the variant achieving dominance by late June 2021.
source: Prevalence of the SARS-CoV-2 Delta variant rose quickly in the US between May and June 2021, with the variant achieving dominance by late June 2021, and accounting for over 90% of all SARS-CoV-2 infections for an extended period from late July to early December 2021 (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, 2021b).
evidence: This is a factual statement about Delta variant prevalence, supported by a CDC citation.

claim: The Delta variant accounted for over 90% of all SARS-CoV-2 infections for an extended period from late July to early December 2021.
source: Prevalence of the SARS-CoV-2 Delta variant rose quickly in the US between May and June 2021, with the variant achieving dominance by late June 2021, and accounting for over 90% of all SARS-CoV-2 infections for an extended period from late July to early December 2021 (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, 2021b).
evidence: This is a factual statement about Delta variant prevalence, supported by a CDC citation.

claim: The rapid case growth observed in July 2021 in multiple US states was surprising, tracking with or above the projections from the worst-case scenario.
source: The rapid case growth observed in July 2021 in multiple US states was surprising, tracking with or above the projections from our worst-case scenario.
evidence: This is a comparison between observed case growth and projections.

claim: Scenarios were designed at the end of June 2021 based on information available at that time about the transmissibility of the Delta variant, vaccine effectiveness, and vaccine coverage.
source: Scenarios were designed at the end of June 2021 based on information available at that time about the transmissibility of the Delta variant, vaccine effectiveness, and vaccine coverage; projections were generated on or before July 4, 2021.
evidence: This is a description of the methodology and timing of the scenario design.

claim: Projections were generated on or before July 4, 2021.
source: Scenarios were designed at the end of June 2021 based on information available at that time about the transmissibility of the Delta variant, vaccine effectiveness, and vaccine coverage; projections were generated on or before July 4, 2021.
evidence: This is a factual statement about when projections were generated.

claim: Possible mechanisms driving the underestimation of the observed Summer 2021 resurgence may include inaccurate assumptions about the transmissibility and severity of Delta, the effectiveness of the vaccines against infection and transmission, waning of natural and vaccine-derived immunity, changes in testing practices, and the interaction of these factors with NPIs and behavior change.
source: Possible mechanisms driving the underestimation of the observed Summer 2021 resurgence may include inaccurate assumptions about the transmissibility and severity of Delta (including changes in serial interval or severity of infection relative to other variants), the effectiveness of the vaccines against infection and transmission, waning of natural and vaccine-derived immunity, changes in testing practices, and the interaction of these factors with NPIs and behavior change (Li et al., 2021; Elliott et al., 2021; Puranik et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a speculative discussion of possible reasons for projection underestimation, supported by citations.

claim: Eight of the nine teams did not include waning of natural or vaccine-derived immunity in their models.
source: Critically, eight of the nine teams did not include waning of natural or vaccine-derived immunity, an assumption that we now know is incorrect. (Higdon et al., 2021)
evidence: This is a factual statement about model assumptions, with a citation indicating this assumption was incorrect.

claim: Absence of waning immunity in the models resulted in a much smaller population susceptible to infection with Delta, thus reducing the overall potential magnitude that could be projected.
source: Yet in this round, absence of waning resulted in a much smaller population susceptible to infection with Delta, thus reducing the overall potential magnitude that could be projected by these models.
evidence: This is an inference about how the absence of waning immunity affected model projections.

claim: Use of NPIs has been substantially reduced across the US, with a lapse in mask mandates in most states.
source: Use of NPIs has been substantially reduced across the US, with a lapse in mask mandates in most states.
evidence: This is a factual statement about NPI policy changes in the US.

claim: Results of prior rounds underscore the effectiveness of NPIs, in combination with increasing vaccination, to moderate the spread of a highly transmissible variant.
source: Although modeled use of NPIs was left to the discretion of individual modeling teams and did not vary between scenarios, results of prior rounds underscore the effectiveness of NPIs, in combination with increasing vaccination, to moderate the spread of a highly transmissible variant (Borchering et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a statement about findings from prior modeling rounds, supported by a citation.

claim: States with younger populations and higher vaccination coverage among older and high-risk populations were expected to experience a relatively lower burden of severe disease, even with resurgences in cases.
source: The impact of the resurgence on severe disease and mortality was expected to vary substantially across states; states with younger populations and higher vaccination coverage among older and high-risk populations were expected to experience a relatively lower burden of severe disease, even with resurgences in cases.
evidence: This is an inference based on demographic and vaccination coverage data.

claim: Several states (for example, South Dakota, North Dakota) with low vaccination coverage were not projected to experience major resurgences, likely because of high naturally acquired immunity.
source: Several states (for example, South Dakota, North Dakota) with low vaccination coverage were not projected to experience major resurgences, likely because of high naturally acquired immunity.
evidence: This is a projection finding with an inferred explanation based on natural immunity.

claim: Observed increases in new vaccinations occurred particularly among young age groups and in jurisdictions most severely impacted by the Delta variant.
source: Observed increases in new vaccinations, particularly among young age groups and in jurisdictions most severely impacted by the Delta variant, was a positive step in this direction (Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, 2021b).
evidence: This is a factual statement about observed vaccination trends, supported by a CDC citation.

claim: Considerable uncertainty is inherent to long-term projections.
source: First, considerable uncertainty is inherent to long-term projections.
evidence: This is a general statement about the nature of long-term projections, based on established knowledge.

claim: The emergence of the Omicron variant in December 2021 could not have been predicted when scenarios were designed in June 2021.
source: As a case in point the emergence of the Omicron variant in December 2021, at the end of our projection period, could not have been predicted when scenarios were designed in June 2021 (Borchering et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a factual statement about the unpredictability of variant emergence, supported by a citation.

claim: A resurgence in Delta variant incidence was observed in mid-fall 2021, possibly due to changes in behavior and waning immunity.
source: Similarly, a resurgence in Delta variant incidence was observed in mid-fall 2021, possibly due to changes in behavior and waning immunity, and is not captured in scenarios or model projections.
evidence: This is a factual statement about observed resurgence with speculative explanation.

claim: There is notable variation among individual model projections with regard to both the timing and the magnitude of the resurgence for a given scenario.
source: Further, for a given scenario, there is notable variation among individual model projections with regard to both the timing and the magnitude of the resurgence (Figure 1—figure supplements 1–3).
evidence: This is a finding about variation among models, with reference to figure supplements.

claim: Variation among models likely reflects differences in model structure, projected vaccine coverage, projected variant growth, and importance of seasonal effects.
source: Variation likely reflects differences in model structure, projected vaccine coverage, projected variant growth, and importance of seasonal effects.
evidence: This is an inference about the sources of variation among models.

claim: Some of the variations among models reflect true scientific uncertainty, making ensemble projections particularly useful to integrate uncertainty between and within individual models.
source: Some of these variations reflect true scientific uncertainty, making ensemble projections particularly useful to integrate uncertainty between and within individual models.
evidence: This is a statement about the value of ensemble approaches, based on reasoning about uncertainty.

claim: Model estimates are dependent on assumptions about vaccine hesitancy, which are informed in part by large-scale surveys of vaccine sentiments.
source: In the same vein, model estimates are dependent on assumptions about vaccine hesitancy, which are informed in part by large-scale surveys of vaccine sentiments (Carnegie Mellon University Delphi Group, 2021; Estimates of Vaccine Hesitancy for COVID-19, 2021).
evidence: This is a statement about model inputs, supported by citations to survey data.

claim: Vaccine hesitancy surveys may underestimate vaccine hesitancy, as coverage estimates among survey respondents are substantially higher than measured among the overall US population.
source: These surveys may underestimate vaccine hesitancy, as coverage estimates among survey respondents are substantially higher than measured among the overall US population.
evidence: This is an inference about potential bias in survey data based on comparison of survey and population data.

claim: The high variant transmissibility scenarios more accurately represented the characteristics of the Delta variant, both in transmissibility and in current case trajectories.
source: The high variant transmissibility scenarios, which more accurately represented the characteristics of the Delta variant, both in transmissibility and in current case trajectories, projected a significant national resurgence with substantial variation in magnitude across states.
evidence: This is a statement about which scenarios better matched the actual Delta variant characteristics.

claim: Resurgences were expected to be more pronounced in low-vaccination jurisdictions.
source: Resurgences were expected to be more pronounced in low-vaccination jurisdictions.
evidence: This is a projection finding from the modeling analysis.

claim: The increased transmissibility of new variants like Delta can continue to challenge our ability to control the pandemic even with substantial vaccination coverage.
source: The projections indicated that even with substantial vaccination coverage, the increased transmissibility of new variants like Delta can continue to challenge our ability to control this pandemic.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the projection results.

claim: Projections of Delta resurgence were made publicly available in early July 2021, 2 months ahead of the peak of the Delta wave.
source: Projections of Delta resurgence presented in this paper were made publicly available in early July 2021 (COVID-19 Scenario Modeling Hub, 2020), 2 months ahead of the peak of the Delta wave, providing actionable results.
evidence: This is a factual statement about when projections were released, supported by a citation.

claim: There is a trade-off between releasing projections in a timely manner to guide decisions, and projection accuracy and uncertainty that improve with incorporation of recent information.
source: There is a trade-off between releasing projections in a timely manner to guide decisions, and projection accuracy and uncertainty that improve with incorporation of recent information.
evidence: This is a general statement about the challenges of projection timing, based on knowledge and experience.

claim: While these projections dramatically underestimated the magnitude of the Delta resurgence, they did provide value in projecting the timing and emphasizing the importance of vaccination.
source: While these projections dramatically underestimated the magnitude of the Delta resurgence, demonstrating the challenges to predict this continually evolving pandemic, they did provide value in projecting the timing and emphasizing the importance of vaccination.
evidence: This is an evaluative statement about the value of the projections despite their limitations.

claim: Multi-model ensemble efforts such as the COVID-19 Scenario Modeling Hub are particularly well-suited to provide disease projections to inform the pandemic response under changing epidemiological and behavioral situations.
source: Multi-model ensemble efforts such as the COVID-19 Scenario Modeling Hub are particularly well-suited to provide disease projections to inform the pandemic response under changing epidemiological and behavioral situations.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the value of multi-model ensemble approaches, based on the experience described in the manuscript.

claim: The COVID-19 Scenario Modeling Hub convened nine modeling teams in an open call to provide six-month projections.
source: The COVID-19 Scenario Modeling Hub (COVID-19 Scenario Modeling Hub, 2020) convened nine modeling teams in an open call to provide six-month (July 3, 2021-January 1, 2022) COVID-19 projections in the US using data available through July 3, 2021.
evidence: This is a description of the methodology, supported by a citation.

claim: Each team developed a model to project weekly reported cases, hospitalizations, and deaths, both nationally and by jurisdiction (50 states and the District of Columbia), for four different epidemiological scenarios.
source: Each team developed a model to project weekly reported cases, hospitalizations, and deaths, both nationally and by jurisdiction (50 states and the District of Columbia), for four different epidemiological scenarios.
evidence: This is a description of the modeling approach.

claim: Models were calibrated against data from the Johns Hopkins Center for Systems Science and Engineering Coronavirus Resource Center and federal databases.
source: Models were calibrated against data from the Johns Hopkins Center for Systems Science and Engineering Coronavirus Resource Center and federal databases (Coronavirus Resource Center, 2020; US Department of Health and Human Services, 2020).
evidence: This is a description of the data sources used for model calibration, supported by citations.

claim: The four scenarios included low and high vaccination hesitancy levels, assuming national vaccination coverage saturation at 80% and 70%, respectively.
source: The four scenarios included low and high vaccination hesitancy levels, assuming national vaccination coverage saturation at 80% and 70%, respectively, based on hesitancy surveys (Table 1) (Carnegie Mellon University Delphi Group, 2021; Estimates of Vaccine Hesitancy for COVID-19, 2021).
evidence: This is a description of the scenario design, with reference to Table 1 and citations to survey data.

claim: Specified vaccine efficacy levels were constant across the scenarios and were based on protection against clinical disease in randomized clinical trials and effectiveness studies.
source: Specified vaccine efficacy levels were constant across the scenarios and were based on protection against clinical disease in randomized clinical trials and effectiveness studies; parameters for effectiveness against infection, transmission, and progression to severe outcomes (for example, death) were left to be specified by each team (COVID-19 Scenario Modeling Hub, 2020).
evidence: This is a description of scenario assumptions, supported by a citation.

claim: When the scenarios were designed in late June 2021, little information was available on vaccine efficacy specific to the Delta variant and on waning immunity.
source: When the scenarios were designed in late June 2021, little information was available on vaccine efficacy specific to the Delta variant and on waning immunity.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the state of knowledge at the time of scenario design.

claim: Scenarios assumed one of two levels of increased transmissibility for the Delta variant: 40% (low) or 60% (high) more transmissible than the Alpha variant.
source: Scenarios assumed one of two levels of increased transmissibility for the Delta variant: 40% (low) or 60% (high) more transmissible than the Alpha variant.
evidence: This is a description of the scenario assumptions.

claim: Increases in new variant prevalence over time were determined by each modeling team and were estimated at the state level.
source: Increases in new variant prevalence over time were determined by each modeling team and were estimated at the state level.
evidence: This is a description of the modeling approach.

claim: Individual projections were combined into an ensemble for each scenario, outcome, week, and location using an equally-weighted linear opinion pool method across teams that trimmed the highest and lowest model at each point and quantile.
source: These individual projections were combined into an ensemble for each scenario, outcome, week, and location using an equally-weighted linear opinion pool method across teams that trimmed the highest and lowest model at each point and quantile (Stone, 1961; Jose et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a description of the ensemble methodology, supported by citations.

claim: Point estimates provided are the median of the ensemble.
source: Point estimates provided here are the median of the ensemble.
evidence: This is a description of how point estimates were calculated.

claim: Averted cases and deaths were calculated as the difference (and ratio) between the median point estimates of the ensemble for the two scenarios.
source: For any given pair of scenarios, averted cases and deaths were calculated as the difference (and ratio) between the median point estimates of the ensemble for the two scenarios.
evidence: This is a description of the methodology for calculating averted outcomes.

claim: Projected resurgences were assessed by taking the ratio of the peak projected median incidence over the projection period to the highest incidence experienced during the winter 2020–2021 period for the same location.
source: Specifically, projected resurgences were assessed by taking the ratio of the peak projected median incidence in a given location over the projection period (July 3, 2021-January 1, 2022) to the highest incidence experienced during the winter 2020–2021 period (defined as October 1, 2020–February 28, 2021) for the same location.
evidence: This is a description of the methodology for assessing resurgence magnitude.

claim: Winter 2020–21 peaks were identified as the seven-day average centered around the day with the highest incident cases from smoothed curves generated through a penalized cubic spline Poisson regression model fit to the incident cases.
source: Winter 2020–21 peaks were identified as the seven-day average centered around the day with the highest incident cases from smoothed curves generated through a penalized cubic spline Poisson regression model fit to the incident cases.
evidence: This is a description of the methodology for identifying historical peaks.

claim: On July 1, 2021, only 13 states and Washington, D.C. had accomplished President Biden's goal for vaccination coverage among eligible populations at or above 70%.
source: At the outset of the Delta wave on July 1, 2021, only 13 states and Washington, D.C. had accomplished President Biden's goal for vaccination coverage among eligible populations at or above 70%.
evidence: This is a factual statement about vaccination coverage at a specific date.
